official_skills.notes: Verified against the repository listing on 2026-08-27. There is no dedicated Next.js caching skill and no dedicated Next.js upgrade skill in this collection; caching guidance lives inside react-best-practices.
Ships bundled with several clients, so an explicit install command may be unnecessary or may differ per client. Check whether it is already available before recommending an install.

gap_map.why_it_matters: The Vercel collection is performance- and design-oriented. Nothing in it decides what deserves a test, so behavior changes ship untested by default.

The most expensive Next.js mistakes are boundary mistakes: data fetched in the wrong place, secrets crossing into a client component, a server action doing no authorization. No listed skill audits that boundary.
gap_map.fallback: The mentor reviews every 'use client' boundary and every server action for authorization on each feature that touches data.

layers.name: unit
layers.belongs_here: a single function, hook or component in isolation - business rules, formatting, reducers
layers.signal_you_picked_wrong: the test mocks fetch, the router and the session just to reach one assertion

layers.name: component
layers.belongs_here: how a component renders, reacts to props, and responds to user events - the presentation rules
layers.does_not_belong_here: async Server Components; tooling support is incomplete
layers.signal_you_picked_wrong: you are asserting the DOM structure instead of the behaviour a user depends on

layers.name: integration
layers.belongs_here: several units working together - components, hooks and functions in one flow
layers.does_not_belong_here: enumerating branches; that is unit work

layers.name: e2e
layers.belongs_here: user flows in a production-like environment, and - per the Next.js team - async Server Components, which unit tooling does not fully support
layers.cost: slowest and most brittle; keep it to flows whose breakage is an incident

layers.name: snapshot
layers.does_not_belong_here: anything you would not review character by character on a diff
layers.cost: cheap to create, expensive to keep honest - snapshots get regenerated unread
layers.signal_you_picked_wrong: the review comment is 'snapshot updated' with no one having looked

testing.proportions: Next.js team: no stated proportions. They do state one placement rule - prefer End-to-End over unit testing for async Server Components, because some tools do not fully support them yet.
rules: Test async Server Components end to end, not with unit tooling. The Next.js team says support is incomplete; a passing unit test there proves less than it appears to.
Read package.json before assuming a runner. Jest, Vitest, Playwright and Cypress are all documented options and the project picked one.
A green build is not a green suite. Run both - next build catches type and import errors that tests never reach.
Test the server/client boundary explicitly: that a server action rejects an unauthorized caller, and that no secret is reachable from a client component.
Regenerating a snapshot without reading the diff is the same failure as regenerating a golden. If nobody reads it, delete the snapshot instead.
traps: Mocking fetch in a component test hides the boundary the test existed to check. If everything server-side is mocked, the test asserts the mock.
async Server Components appear testable under unit tooling and quietly do not behave the way they do at runtime.
Caching makes a test pass against a stale value: a test that reads through the framework cache can pass after the underlying data changed.
Snapshot tests turn a real regression into a diff people approve without reading.
A component test that renders a client component pulls its whole import graph, so a passing test says nothing about the bundle it just grew.
what_not_to_test: That a page renders without crashing, with no assertion about what it shows.
Framework behaviour: that a layout wraps a page, that a route group does not affect the URL.
Exact DOM structure. It changes on every markup refactor and asserts implementation.
testing.notes: Runner varies by project (vitest, jest, node:test). Read package.json scripts before assuming a command; never guess it. A green build is not a green suite - run both.

growth_thresholds.extract_component_library: >=3 occurrences of the same component across >=2 routes or features
growth_thresholds.split_feature: a route segment folder exceeds 15 files
growth_thresholds.extract_package: >=2 apps or features import the same internal module
growth_thresholds.split_client_boundary: a client component tree exceeds 3 levels of prop drilling

architecture.pattern: none - the Next.js team is explicitly unopinionated about organisation

layers.name: Route segment (app/)
layers.holds: layout, page, loading, error, not-found, route - the routing surface. A route is not public until page or route exists, so anything else colocated here is safe.
layers.must_not: hold logic that a route handler or server action does not need; colocation is permitted, not a licence to put the domain in app/

layers.name: Server boundary
layers.holds: data access, secrets, authorization. Only what page/route returns reaches the client.
layers.must_not: leak a secret or an unauthorized query across a 'use client' boundary - this is the most expensive mistake in the stack and nothing warns you

layers.name: Client components
layers.must_not: become the default; every 'use client' pushes its whole import graph to the browser

layers.name: Shared code
layers.holds: components and lib code used by more than one route
layers.must_not: exist as a folder before a second route needs it

variants.name: Project files outside app/
variants.use_when: you want app/ to be purely routing and everything else in root folders
variants.cost: a feature's UI, data and route live in three places; renaming a feature touches all three

variants.name: Project files in top-level folders inside app/
variants.use_when: small app, one team, everything shared
variants.cost: the shared folders become the whole app and stop meaning anything

variants.name: Split by feature or route
variants.use_when: features are genuinely independent; globally shared code stays at the app root and the rest colocates in the segment that uses it
variants.cost: you must decide, per file, whether it is shared - and that decision gets made badly under deadline

rules: Next.js is unopinionated about structure, so the project must state its strategy and stay consistent. The framework team's own guidance is to pick one and be consistent - an inconsistent codebase is the failure mode here, not the wrong choice.
A route is not public until page.js or route.js exists, so colocation inside app/ is safe. Use it before inventing a parallel folder tree.
Use a private folder (_folder) for anything non-routable that could collide with a future Next.js file convention.
Use route groups ((group)) to organise or to give a subset of routes its own layout. They do not change the URL.
Every 'use client' is a boundary decision, not a formality: it ships its import graph to the browser. Push it as far down the tree as the interactivity actually needs.
Every server action and route handler states its authorization decision explicitly, including 'public on purpose'. An unguarded handler looks exactly like an intentionally public one.
architecture.component_library: Promote to shared at >=3 occurrences across >=2 routes or features. Below that, colocate in the segment that uses it - the framework makes colocation safe precisely so you do not have to decide early.
architecture.notes: The docs name three organisation strategies and decline to recommend one: 'choose a strategy that works for you and your team and be consistent across the project.' The mentor's job here is not to pick for the user - it is to make sure a choice is made, written down, and followed.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: The Next.js team is explicitly unopinionated and names three strategies without recommending one. Nothing picks for you.
key_decisions.reasonable_default: Split by feature or route: colocate what one route uses, keep genuinely shared code at the app root.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: The real cost is not the wrong choice, it is an inconsistent one. Half a codebase per-feature and half by-type means nobody can predict where a file lives.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: Static, dynamic and revalidated rendering are per-route decisions, and the default is not obvious from the code.
key_decisions.reasonable_default: Static unless the route needs per-request data; make dynamic an explicit decision, not an accident.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: A route that went dynamic by accident costs on every request and shows stale or personalised data to the wrong people.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: 'use client' is a per-file choice with no framework guardrail, and it is transitive over the import graph.
options: client boundary at the page level
key_decisions.reasonable_default: As deep in the tree as the interactivity actually needs.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: A boundary set too high ships the whole subtree to the browser and can carry a secret with it. Moving it down later means rewriting the data flow.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: Server actions and route handlers both work, and they have different authorization and error-handling shapes.
key_decisions.reasonable_default: Server actions for form-driven mutations; route handlers when a non-browser client also calls it.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: Mixed conventions mean authorization is enforced in two places and forgotten in one.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: Which Next.js features are available depends on where it runs; a static export cannot do what a Node server can.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: Discovering at deploy time that the target does not support a feature you built on means rewriting those routes.

failure_boundaries: fetch in server components and route handlers
operability.observability: instrumentation.ts is the framework's own hook for OpenTelemetry and instrumentation - use it rather than inventing a place.
operability.authorization: Enforced inside the server action or route handler itself. A check in a layout or a client component is not a control: the action is independently callable.
done_checks: clean install from a fresh clone
rules: Every server action authorizes itself. It is a public endpoint whatever the UI does.
No secret reachable from a module that any 'use client' file imports, transitively.
Every async view declares loading, empty and error states - the framework gives loading.tsx and error.tsx for exactly this.
Every outbound fetch states a timeout. The platform will cut the request before your code notices.
Instrumentation goes in instrumentation.ts, not scattered across route handlers.

dead_code_risks: Route files, layouts, loading and error boundaries - reachable by filesystem convention, never by import
generateStaticParams, generateMetadata and other convention-named exports
Server actions referenced only from a form action attribute
Components referenced only via next/dynamic with a string path
Public API surface of a workspace package consumed by another workspace
